chapters.title: Chapter 5: Tax, Tracking, and Your Deal Checklist

lessons.title: The Investor's Deal Checklist: Hold, Tender, or Exit?

children.text: You now know how deals are structured, approved, priced, taxed and tracked. What remains is the only question that ever mattered: when a company you own is part of a deal, do you hold, tender or exit? This closing lesson turns everything in the course into one decision framework you can apply to any announcement, in any sector, for the rest of your investing life.

body.text: A deal is not an event to react to. It is a change in what you own. Ask what business you will hold when the dust settles, what it is worth, and whether you would buy it today at that price. If the answer is yes, do nothing. If it is no, exit deliberately and tax-efficiently.

children.text: Your Options, Event by Event

body.caption: What you can actually do in each situation

cells: Company you own is merging into another
Hold through the merger, or sell in the market before the record date
Do you want to own the surviving company at the implied value?
Company you own is the acquirer
Hold, add or reduce
Do realistic synergies exceed the premium, and can the balance sheet carry the deal?
Company you own receives an open offer
Tender, hold, or sell in the market
Is the offer price above the market price, and do you trust the new controlling shareholder?
Company you own is being delisted
Bid in the reverse book building, sell in the market, or use the exit window later
At what price are you genuinely happy to leave?
Company you own announces a demerger
Hold both, keep one, or exit both after listing
Would you buy each business separately today?
Company you own announces a buyback
Tender or ignore
After the post-2024 dividend tax treatment, does tendering beat selling in the market at your slab rate?

children.text: The Four Questions
What will I own?

Identify the surviving or resulting company, the ratio, and what percentage of the combined or separated business you will hold. A housing finance shareholder became a bank shareholder. A conglomerate shareholder became the owner of two very different stocks.
What is it worth?
Use the tool that fits: implied value for a share swap, the offer price against the market price for a cash offer, sum of the parts for a demerger, and synergies against premium for the acquirer.
What can go wrong?

List the pending approvals, the conditions, the debt being taken on and the integration risk. Remember that Zee's merger died after NCLT sanction, and that the HDFC merger's funding squeeze was visible on announcement day.
What does acting cost me?
Capital gains tax, the ₹1.25 lakh annual exemption you may be using up, brokerage, and the risk of selling into temporary post-listing weakness.

body.text: Notice that only the fourth question is about the deal event itself. The first three are ordinary investing questions: what is the business, what is it worth, what could go wrong. A deal is not a special category of decision. It just forces you to answer those questions on someone else's timetable.

children.text: Running the Numbers on a Tender Decision

Return to the open offer from Lesson 2.3. The offer is ₹465, the market price during tendering is ₹448, and you hold 1,000 shares. You expect about half your shares to be accepted, and you expect the price to settle near ₹435 once the offer closes.

body.caption: Tendering everything is usually free, so the real comparison is this blended outcome against simply selling in the market today.

body.title: Tender everything, then what?
body.prompt: You tender all 1,000 shares. 500 are accepted at ₹465, and you later sell the remaining 500 at ₹435. What is your average realisation per share, in rupees?
body.explanation: (500 × ₹465) + (500 × ₹435) = ₹2,32,500 + ₹2,17,500 = ₹4,50,000, or ₹450 per share. Compared with selling all 1,000 today at ₹448, tendering adds only ₹2 per share, and that assumes your guesses about acceptance and the post-offer price are right. If you want out, selling in the market is simpler and certain. If you want to stay invested, do not tender at all.

body.text: Never tender a part of your holding because you cannot decide. Partial tendering under proportionate acceptance gives you a random outcome, not a compromise. Decide whether you want to own the company under its new owner, then act on all your shares in one direction.

children.text: The Portfolio Question Everyone Forgets
Mergers concentrate your portfolio and demergers fragment it. Both need a look at position sizes afterwards, including exposure you hold indirectly through mutual funds.

body.title: After the merger, how much do you sell?
body.prompt: Your equity portfolio is worth ₹20 lakh. You hold ₹3 lakh of the acquirer and ₹2 lakh of the target, which merge into a single holding. Your own rule caps any single stock at 15% of the portfolio. How much of the merged holding must you sell to get back within your rule, in rupees?
body.explanation: The merged holding is ₹5 lakh, which is 25% of ₹20 lakh. Your 15% cap allows ₹3 lakh, so ₹2 lakh must move elsewhere. Sell it gradually and check the tax: long-term gains use your ₹1.25 lakh annual exemption, so spreading the sale across two tax years may cost less.

body.title: Reasons to stay vs reasons to exit after a deal

columns.label: Reasons to stay
points: You would buy the surviving or resulting company today at its current price
The deal strengthens the business you liked in the first place
Management has a track record of delivering on acquisitions
Selling would trigger a large tax bill and break a long compounding position
Post-listing weakness looks mechanical rather than fundamental

columns.label: Reasons to exit
points: The business you now own does not match why you invested
The acquirer overpaid, or funded the deal with debt it cannot carry
The new controlling shareholder has weak governance
The position has become too large or too small for your portfolio
You need the money for a goal within a few years

body.title: A full price from a weak buyer
body.question: A fictional mid-cap you own for its cash generation is being acquired at a 40% premium, entirely in the shares of a heavily indebted acquirer with a poor record of integrating acquisitions. The swap ratio is fixed and the scheme will take about a year. What is the most sensible response?
options: Hold to the record date, because the premium means you gain either way
Recognise that the fixed ratio makes you an owner of the acquirer from now on, and decide whether you want that. If not, sell in the market rather than waiting
Buy more of the target, because the premium guarantees a profit
Tender in an open offer, which every merger automatically provides
body.explanation: Once the ratio is fixed, the target tracks the acquirer's price, so the 40% premium can shrink if the acquirer falls. A merger gives no open offer, and holding to the record date simply hands you shares in a company you do not want. If you do not like the acquirer, the market is your exit, and the spread you give up is the price of certainty.

children.text: Anchoring on the pre-deal price.
After a demerger, the parent's lower price is not a loss, and after a merger, the old share count is irrelevant. Judge the combined value.
Treating new shares as free.
Demerger shares were already yours through the parent. Free shares do not exist.
Panic selling on listing day.
Index funds and unwilling holders sell for mechanical reasons in the first days. That is not information about the business.
Chasing delisting and arbitrage bets.
Small, capped gains with large downside if the deal fails suit professionals with many positions, not a concentrated retail portfolio.
Believing the synergy number.
Revenue synergies in particular are estimates by people who want the deal approved. Discount them and check back a year later.

body.title: The default answer
body.textWithBlank: If you would happily buy the surviving or resulting company today at its current price, the right action in most deals is to do ___.
body.explanation: Doing nothing is a decision, and usually the cheapest one. It avoids tax, brokerage and the risk of selling into temporary weakness. Act only when the business you now own no longer fits your reasons for owning it.

body.title: Capstone: three deals in one portfolio
body.scenario: Meera, 38, has a ₹30 lakh equity portfolio built for long-term growth, plus index funds. Three things happen in one quarter. First, a bank she owns worth ₹4 lakh announces it will absorb a large NBFC, which will lift the combined loan book well above its deposits. Second, a conglomerate she owns worth ₹3 lakh announces a demerger of its weakest division at 1 for 4, with the parent keeping no stake. Third, a small-cap she owns worth ₹1.5 lakh receives an open offer at ₹520 from a well-regarded group, while the stock trades at ₹506.
body.prompt: Work through each situation using the four questions, and say what you would do.
body.modelAnswer:
The bank: she will own a larger bank with a stretched credit-deposit ratio, the pattern from Lesson 3.4. Value depends on how fast deposits catch up, and the risk is slower loan growth and margin pressure for a year or two. Nothing needs to be done today if she is a long-term holder, but she should track deposit growth each quarter and watch her total banking exposure, including index funds.

The demerger: she will own two stocks, one of them the weakest division, with no parent stake to anchor it. She should build a rough sum of the parts before the record date, check how debt is split, and expect selling pressure when the new company lists. A reasonable plan is to hold through listing, avoid selling in the first volatile days, then decide on the smaller company on its own merits.

The open offer: the offer is ₹520 against ₹506, a premium of about 2.8%. Because the acquirer is well regarded, the real question is whether she wants to stay invested under the new owner. If yes, ignore the offer. If no, tender all her shares and sell any returned shares in the market. Partial tendering to hedge her indecision is the one clearly poor choice.

Across all three: her cost and holding periods carry over in the merger and demerger, so no tax arises until she sells. If she does sell anything, she should track her total long-term gains against the ₹1.25 lakh exemption and correct the cost split on the demerger shares before filing.

children.text: The Whole Course on One Page

cells: Scheme shareholder approval
Majority in number and 75% in value of votes cast
Objecting to a scheme at the NCLT
10% of shares or 5% of debt
Open offer triggers
25% of shares, 5% creeping in a year, or control
Minimum open offer size
26% of total shares
Delisting success threshold
Acquirer reaching 90%
Delisting exit window
One year after delisting
Value created by a deal
PV of synergies minus premium paid
All-stock accretion rule
P/E paid below the acquirer's P/E
Entitlement to demerger shares
Buy by the trading day before the record date
Long-term listed equity gains
12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh a year

body.title: The master deal checklist
steps: Read the primary filing on BSE or NSE, not the headline
Classify the deal: merger, acquisition, demerger, open offer, delisting or buyback
Work out exactly what you will own afterwards, and in what proportion
Value it: implied value, offer price against market price, or sum of the parts
Test the stated synergies against the premium being paid
List every pending approval, condition and deadline
Check the balance sheet the deal creates, including debt and key regulatory ratios
Vote when a scheme comes to you, especially where public shareholder votes decide it
Plan the tax before acting, including the cost split and your annual exemption
Review position sizes, including exposure through mutual funds, once shares are credited
Revisit a year later: did the promised synergies arrive?

body.label: Screener.in
body.description: Your one-page starting point for any deal: announcements, quarterly results, shareholding pattern, borrowings and ROCE for both sides of the transaction.

cards.definition: What business will I own after this deal, and in what proportion?

cards.term: Merger with a fixed swap ratio
cards.definition: You are effectively an owner of the acquirer from announcement day.
Compare the offer price with the live market price, allow for proportionate acceptance, and decide whether you want the new owner.
Judge each resulting company separately, after listing, not on the record date.
Bid the price at which you would genuinely be happy to exit, not a hopeful number.
Do nothing, unless the business you now own no longer matches why you invested.
Check cost carryover, the cost split and your ₹1.25 lakh annual exemption before selling.

points: Ask four questions for every deal: what will I own, what is it worth, what can go wrong, and what does acting cost me.
A fixed swap ratio makes you an owner of the acquirer from announcement day, so decide on the acquirer, not the target.
In an open offer, compare the offer price with the market price, allow for proportionate acceptance, and act on your whole holding in one direction.
After a demerger, judge each company separately once both are trading, rather than reacting on the record date or listing day.
Mergers concentrate portfolios and demergers fragment them, so review position sizes including mutual fund overlap.
Doing nothing is usually the cheapest correct answer. Exit only when the business you now own no longer fits your reasons for owning it.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Meera and the companies in the examples are fictional, and all prices are illustrative. Thresholds and tax rules summarised here are simplified and change over time. Decisions about your own portfolio should account for your goals, risk tolerance and tax position, ideally with a SEBI registered investment adviser or a qualified chartered accountant.
